summary: Sync Core Data and SwiftData stores across devices using event sourcing.
title: Ensembles
rawIndexableTextContent: Sync Core Data and SwiftData stores across devices using event sourcing. Overview Ensembles synchronizes persistent stores by recording local saves as events, exchanging them through a pluggable cloud backend, and replaying them on each peer to reach eventual consistency. It works with both Core Data and SwiftData. An ensemble monitors a single persistent store. When the app saves, Ensembles captures the changes automatically. Calling sync() downloads remote events, replays them into the local store, and uploads new local events. Conflicts are resolved through causal revision tracking, with delegate hooks for custom repair logic. Quick Start — SwiftData The simplest way to add sync to a SwiftData app is with SwiftDataEnsembleContainer:  See SwiftData Integration for the full guide, including model versioning with VersionedSchema. Quick Start — Core Data For Core Data apps, use CoreDataEnsembleContainer:  For more control, use CoreDataEnsemble directly:  Cloud Backends Ensembles ships with several cloud backends: CloudKitFileSystem — Syncs via iCloud using CloudKit. GoogleDriveCloudFileSystem — Syncs via Google Drive REST API v3. OneDriveCloudFileSystem — Syncs via Microsoft OneDrive (Graph API v1.0). PCloudCloudFileSystem — Syncs via pCloud, a Swiss provider with strong privacy guarantees. WebDAVCloudFileSystem — Syncs via any WebDAV server (Nextcloud, ownCloud, etc.). ICloudDriveFileSystem — Syncs via iCloud Drive (legacy — prefer CloudKit for new projects). EncryptedCloudFileSystem — Wraps any backend with AES-256-GCM encryption. LocalCloudFileSystem — Uses a local directory, useful for testing or shared-folder sync. MemoryCloudFileSystem — An in-memory actor-based backend for unit testing. Any storage that can hold files at paths can serve as a backend. See Custom Cloud Backends for a guide to implementing your own. Backward Compatibility Ensembles 3 reads and writes Ensembles 2 cloud data and event store formats. Existing apps can migrate without a data reset. See Migrating from Ensembles 2 for a step-by-step guide.

rawIndexableTextContent: Implement the CloudFileSystem protocol to sync via any storage service. Overview Ensembles exchanges sync data through a CloudFileSystem — a protocol that abstracts file storage behind a simple path-based API. Any service that can store and retrieve files at paths can serve as a backend: cloud storage (S3, Google Cloud Storage), file servers (WebDAV, SFTP), databases, or even peer-to-peer connections with a local cache. The CloudFileSystem Protocol The core protocol has 8 requirements organized into four groups: Connection  isConnected — Return whether the backend is ready for operations. connect() — Establish a connection. Called before each attach or merge. fetchUserIdentity() — Return a token identifying the current user, or nil if identity tracking is not supported. Ensembles uses this to detect account changes (e.g., signing out of iCloud). File Operations  Paths are forward-slash separated, rooted at /. The ensemble creates a directory structure like /MyEnsemble/events/, /MyEnsemble/baselines/, etc. Directory listings should return CloudFile or CloudDirectory items with their path and name populated. Only list immediate children — do not recurse. File Transfer  Upload copies a local file to the remote path. Download copies a remote file to the local path. Both paths are absolute on their respective systems (local paths are filesystem paths; remote paths are within the cloud file system’s namespace). A Minimal Example Here is a skeleton implementation to illustrate the structure:  Reference Implementations Study the built-in backends as starting points: MemoryCloudFileSystem (in EnsemblesMemory) — The simplest implementation. An actor that stores files in a dictionary. Good for understanding the protocol’s expectations. LocalCloudFileSystem (in EnsemblesLocalFile) — Uses FileManager to store files in a local directory. Shows how to map the protocol onto a real file system. CloudKitFileSystem (in EnsemblesCloudKit) — A production backend using CloudKit. Shows how to implement batch operations and setup hooks. PCloudCloudFileSystem (in EnsemblesPCloud) — A URLSession-based REST client with no SDK dependency. A good model for building backends against any REST API. BoxCloudFileSystem (in EnsemblesBox) — Wraps the Box Swift SDK. Demonstrates how to bridge an ID-based API (where files are identified by numeric IDs, not paths) onto the path-based CloudFileSystem protocol using folder-walking and caching. S3CloudFileSystem (in EnsemblesS3) — Wraps the AWS SDK for Swift. Shows how to simulate directory semantics on a flat key-value store using key prefixes and delimiters. EnsemblesBox and EnsemblesS3 (along with EnsemblesDropbox, EnsemblesZip, and EnsemblesMultipeer) require an external SDK. With the source distribution, enabling the corresponding package trait resolves this automatically. With the binary distribution (XCFrameworks), you must add the external SDK as a separate package dependency — see the Available Backends table in the README for details. Optional: Batch Operations If your backend can handle multiple files in a single request (reducing round trips), adopt CloudFileSystemBatchOperations:  The fileUploadMaximumBatchSize and fileDownloadMaximumBatchSize properties control how many files Ensembles passes per batch call. Default is 10 if you don’t override them. Optional: Setup Hooks For backends that need initialization, caching, or repair logic, adopt CloudFileSystemSetup:  Threading and Sendable Cloud file systems must conform to Sendable. If your implementation uses mutable state, you have several options: Use actor isolation (as MemoryCloudFileSystem does) Use @unchecked Sendable with explicit locking (as LocalCloudFileSystem does) Make the type stateless, delegating state to a thread-safe service All protocol methods are async throws, so you can freely call async APIs in your implementation.

rawIndexableTextContent: A protocol for model types that declare how to derive a global identifier for Ensembles deduplication.   Overview Global identifiers let Ensembles recognize when objects created independently on different devices represent the same logical entity, and merge them instead of duplicating. There are two ways to provide a global identifier: Simple: Single Property Override globalIdentifierKey with the name of a stored property:  Advanced: Computed Identifier (Core Data) Override globalIdentifier(from:) for compound or computed identifiers. The parameter is typed as Self, so you get direct property access:  globalIdentifier(from:) only works with NSManagedObject subclasses (Core Data). For SwiftData models, use globalIdentifierKey instead. A global identifier must never change once it has been assigned to an object. Changing an identifier after sync has begun will cause Ensembles to treat the object as a different entity, leading to duplicates or data loss. Use a value that is set once at creation time, such as a UUID string. A UUID is usually the best choice for a global identifier. Use a fixed, meaningful value (like a name) only for singleton objects or reference data like tags, where two devices might independently create the same logical object. When model types conform to Syncable, CoreDataEnsembleContainer and SwiftDataEnsembleContainer discover the identifiers automatically — no delegate or closure needed.

rawIndexableTextContent: Set up Ensembles to sync a Core Data or SwiftData persistent store across devices. Overview Ensembles synchronizes SQLite stores by recording local changes as events and exchanging them through a cloud backend. It works with both Core Data and SwiftData. Using SwiftData? See SwiftData Integration for a complete guide — you never need to touch Core Data directly. This guide covers Core Data setup, starting with a complete working example using CoreDataEnsembleContainer. Develop with Claude Code If you use Claude Code, install the Ensembles skill first. It teaches Claude the API, the cloud backends, Ensembles 2 → 3 migration, the seed policy, and the common pitfalls, so it writes correct setup code and diagnoses sync issues without hand-holding:  Add Ensembles to Your Project Add the Ensembles package to your Package.swift or via Xcode’s package dependencies:  Import the core module and one cloud backend:  Complete Example: Core Data with CloudKit Here’s a complete, working setup for a SwiftUI app that syncs via CloudKit. This uses CoreDataEnsembleContainer, which creates the Core Data stack for you and syncs automatically. 1. Create Your Core Data Model In Xcode, add a .xcdatamodeld file to your project (e.g., Model.xcdatamodeld). Define your entities as usual. For this example, we’ll assume a Note entity with title (String) and uniqueID (String) attributes. 2. Define Your Model with `Syncable` For deduplication, conform your NSManagedObject subclass to the Syncable protocol and specify which property holds the global identifier. A UUID assigned at creation time is usually the best choice:  A global identifier must never change once it has been assigned. Changing it after sync has begun will cause duplicates or data loss. Use a fixed, meaningful value instead of a UUID for singleton objects or reference data like tags, where two devices might independently create the same logical object. 3. Set Up the Container  That’s the complete setup. The container discovers Syncable conformances automatically, attaches to the cloud, and begins syncing. Remote changes are merged into viewContext so your UI stays up to date. 4. Respond to Events (Optional)  Using a Custom Store Location If you need control over where the SQLite file lives, pass an explicit storeURL:  Working with an Existing Core Data Stack If you already have an NSPersistentContainer, pass it in directly:  Or if you have an existing NSManagedObjectContext:  Auto-Sync Configuration Control when syncing occurs with AutoSyncPolicy:  Set autoSyncPolicy to .manual and call sync() yourself for full control over timing. Backward Compatibility with Ensembles 2 If you’re transitioning from Ensembles 2 and some users may still be on E2, set the compatibility mode:  This restricts exports to formats that Ensembles 2 peers can parse. Switch to .ensembles3 (the default) once all users have upgraded. The Manual Way: CoreDataEnsemble For more control over the sync lifecycle, use CoreDataEnsemble directly. This is useful when you need to manage attach/detach timing, handle specific delegate methods, or integrate with a complex Core Data stack. Create and Attach  The ensembleIdentifier must be the same on all devices that should sync together. If you have multiple persistent stores, create one ensemble per store with a unique identifier. Avoid saving to the persistent store while attaching. If a save is detected, attachment will fail with an error and you will need to retry. Sync Changes Call sync(options:) periodically — for example, when the app enters the foreground, on a timer, or in response to a push notification:  A sync downloads remote events, replays them into the local store, and uploads new local events. Sync errors are usually transient — just retry later. Handle the Delegate Implement CoreDataEnsembleDelegate to respond to sync events. The most important method merges remote changes into your main context:  If your NSManagedObject subclasses conform to Syncable, you don’t need to implement globalIdentifiersForManagedObjects — the ensemble discovers identifier properties automatically. You only need the delegate method if you use CoreDataEnsemble directly without CoreDataEnsembleContainer. Other delegate methods let you: Inspect and repair merge data before it’s committed (shouldSaveMergedChangesIn:reparationContext:) Handle save failures during merging (didFailToSaveMergedChangesIn:error:reparationContext:) React to forced detaches caused by identity changes or data corruption (didDetachWithError:) See Conflict Resolution for more on conflict handling and the reparation context. Detach To stop syncing, detach from the cloud:  This removes local sync data (event logs and metadata). The persistent store itself is not affected. You can re-attach later to resume syncing. Seed Policies The SeedPolicy parameter controls how existing data in the store is handled during attachment: SeedPolicy.mergeAllData (default) — Imports local data so it can be merged with data from other devices. SeedPolicy.excludeLocalData — Ignores local data. Use this when you want to start fresh from cloud data. Sync Options For advanced control, pass SyncOptions:  Process Pending Changes On iOS, the app may be suspended before Ensembles finishes recording a save. Call processPendingChanges() — for example, in a background task — to ensure all changes are fully stored:  Monitor Activity Track long-running operations via currentActivity and activityProgress, or observe these notifications: coreDataEnsembleDidBeginActivity — An activity started coreDataEnsembleDidMakeProgressWithActivity — Progress updated (includes SyncingPhase or AttachingPhase) coreDataEnsembleWillEndActivity — An activity finished (may include an error)

title: Migrating from Ensembles 2
rawIndexableTextContent: Transition an existing Ensembles 2 (Objective-C) app to Ensembles 3. Overview Ensembles 3 is fully backward compatible with Ensembles 2 cloud data — existing cloud files and CloudKit records are all readable by E3 out of the box, so a migrated device picks up the rest of the ensemble’s history from the cloud on its first sync. The local event store does not carry across; see What Resets on Migration below. What’s Backward Compatible Cloud files — The directory structure and file formats in the cloud are identical. E3 reads all E2 cloud data. JSON format — Property change values use the same JSON serialization. CloudKit records — Record types (CDEFileSystemNode, CDEItem, CDEDataFile) and field names are preserved. Encryption — E3’s .legacy encryption format (RNCryptor v3) matches E2’s CDEEncryptedCloudFileSystem. Reading E2 data works regardless of compatibility mode — compatibility mode only restricts what E3 exports. What Resets on Migration The local event store does not carry across. E3 uses a different on-disk database format (raw SQLite vs. E2’s Core Data store), and there is no automatic conversion. On the first call to attachPersistentStore(seedPolicy:) after the swap, E3 deletes the existing event-data directory and registers as a fresh peer with the cloud. Your app’s persistent store (your own Core Data or SwiftData SQLite) is untouched — only Ensembles’ internal event-tracking database is reset. Practically, this means: A new CoreDataEnsemble/persistentStoreIdentifier is generated, so to the cloud and to other peers the migrated device looks like a new device joining the ensemble. E3 pulls the current baseline from the cloud and integrates it, so the user’s data ends up consistent with the rest of the ensemble. The user’s data is not at risk: the attach imports the entire local store (with the default SeedPolicy.mergeAllData) and merges it with the cloud by global identifier, so local changes survive even if the E2 build never got to upload them. The one thing that cannot carry across is an unsynced deletion: an object deleted in E2 whose deletion event never reached the cloud no longer exists in the local store, so the re-import cannot know about it, and the object returns from the cloud after migration. If clean deletions matter for your migration window, have the E2 build sync to completion before the upgrade; otherwise migration order doesn’t matter. The first attach also produces a forced detach with EnsembleError.cloudIdentityChanged — see step 5 below. Transformable Attributes If your model has a transformable attribute (for example a CLLocation stored via a value transformer), E3 reads the value E2 wrote: the value is archived to Data and stored as a base64 blob in the cloud event. There is no format-level migration to do. (Note: Ensembles 2 base64-encodes those blobs in line-wrapped form; reading them correctly requires Ensembles 3 3.0.0 or later — earlier builds dropped line-wrapped transformable values on import, which surfaced as the attribute arriving nil on the E3 device.) A couple of things to get right: Use a named transformer. Give the attribute a valueTransformerName in your model and an NSSecureUnarchiveFromDataTransformer subclass that lists the stored class in allowedTopLevelClasses. Mark the class @objc(YourTransformerName) so the runtime name matches the model. This is the same setup E2 used.  Register before sync, on every launch, on every device. Transformer registration is a process-global table that does not persist, so call register() early — at the top of application(_:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions:) or your App init(), before you create the ensemble. If the transformer is missing when E3 integrates a remote event, the attribute decodes to nil and that nil merges into the local store, blanking the value. With verbose logging on (setLoggingLevel(_:) with .verbose), the line to look for is Failed to retrieve value transformer:. A blank Transformer field works, with a caveat. If you leave the model’s Transformer field empty, E3 falls back to a secure unarchive that allows the attribute’s declared value class plus the Foundation property-list types. A value whose class is neither (and with no declared value class on the attribute) decodes to nil rather than being deserialized. A non-decodable or foreign blob always degrades to nil and logs; it never crashes. For a custom class, prefer a named transformer so the class is explicitly allowlisted. Step-by-Step Migration 1. Swap the dependency Replace the Ensembles 2 CocoaPod or framework with the Ensembles 3 Swift package:  Or add it via Xcode’s Add Package Dependencies menu. 2. Set compatibility mode If some users may still be running the E2 version of your app, set CompatibilityMode.ensembles2Compatible so E3 restricts its exports to formats E2 peers can parse:  3. Match your existing CloudKit zone (CloudKit users only) If your existing E2 fleet uses CloudKitFileSystem, the most important thing to get right is which initializer you call. Both E2 and E3 expose two private-database initializers, and they pick different CloudKit zones: Initializer Zone init(ubiquityContainerIdentifier:rootDirectory:usePublicDatabase:schemaVersion:) CloudKit’s default zone (_defaultZone) init(privateDatabaseForUbiquityContainerIdentifier:schemaVersion:) Custom zone com.mentalfaculty.ensembles.zone.schema2  Your E3 build must use the same initializer as the E2 build it is replacing. If the two devices end up in different zones they cannot see each other’s records, even though they are pointed at the same iCloud container with the same schema version. The symptom is ❌ SYNC ERROR Code: 2 - Description: Failed to fetch some records on the still-E2 devices, with the repair path’s “Located some items in CloudKit without data” log. To find out which zone your E2 fleet is on, look at the CDECloudKitFileSystem init in your existing E2 source. If it calls initWithUbiquityContainerIdentifier:rootDirectory:usePublicDatabase:schemaVersion:, you’re on the default zone — call the matching E3 init. If it calls initWithPrivateDatabaseForUbiquityContainerIdentifier:schemaVersion:, you’re on the custom zone — call the matching E3 init. Don’t switch initializers as part of the migration; switch only after the entire fleet is on E3. 4. Update API names Ensembles 3 uses different class and method names: Ensembles 2 (Objective-C) Ensembles 3 (Swift) CDEPersistentStoreEnsemble CoreDataEnsemble CDEPersistentStoreEnsembleDelegate CoreDataEnsembleDelegate leechPersistentStore(...) CoreDataEnsemble/attachPersistentStore() deleechPersistentStore(...) detachPersistentStore() mergeWithCompletion: sync(options:) CDECloudFileSystem CloudFileSystem CDEEncryptedCloudFileSystem EncryptedCloudFileSystem CDECloudKitFileSystem CloudKitFileSystem CDEICloudFileSystem ICloudDriveFileSystem (module EnsemblesiCloudDrive) CDELocalCloudFileSystem LocalCloudFileSystem CDEMultipeerCloudFileSystem MultipeerCloudFileSystem (package trait Multipeer)  A note on the iCloud Drive backend: ICloudDriveFileSystem is deprecated in favor of CloudKit for new apps, but it is fully supported and exists precisely so an E2 app that syncs via CDEICloudFileSystem can migrate against the same cloud data. Do not switch backends as part of the migration — a backend is a separate cloud location, so switching resets sync data for the fleet. Keep iCloud Drive while migrating; if you later want CloudKit, plan it as its own coordinated transition. 5. Handle the first-launch identity detach On the first launch after migrating from E2, expect a forced detach with EnsembleError.cloudIdentityChanged (code 202). The first attach in E3 wipes the existing E2 event store and registers a fresh peer, but the cached cloud identity token is not carried across either. The first identity check after attach sees no stored token, treats it as an account change, and forces a detach. Re-attaching immediately captures the current identity and steady state resumes. If your app responds to coreDataEnsemble(_:didDetachWithError:) by disabling sync, every migrating user will silently lose sync until they toggle it back on. Handle this case explicitly:  The same pattern applies to EnsembleError.hardwareIdentityChanged and EnsembleError.storeUnregistered in general — all three are recoverable by re-attaching. Errors like EnsembleError.dataCorruptionDetected do warrant disabling sync until the user intervenes. 6. Test thoroughly Verify your app can read existing cloud data from E2 peers. Confirm that E2 peers can still read data exported by your E3 build (while in .ensembles2Compatible mode). Test attachment, sync, and detach cycles. Test the first-launch reset on a device that previously ran E2 — including the EnsembleError.cloudIdentityChanged recovery path. 7. Switch to full E3 mode Once all users have upgraded to the E3 version of your app, change the compatibility mode so future E3-only features become available:  Only flip back to .ensembles3 once your E2 fleet is gone. Today the practical effect is small — the only wire-level difference is gated by compressModelHashes, which defaults to false even in .ensembles3 mode, so until you opt in to that flag the two modes produce identical exports. But if any E3 device starts producing compressed-hash exports, E2 peers can’t parse them and stop receiving updates from that device — effectively forcing the E2 holdouts to upgrade. Two E3 devices in different compatibility modes (one CompatibilityMode.ensembles2Compatible, one CompatibilityMode.ensembles3) sync with each other normally — the mode setting only restricts writes; reads handle both formats unconditionally. Mixing modes within an E3 fleet is safe. Coming from the Idiomatic Sample (`IDMSyncManager`) Many Ensembles 1.x and 2 apps are structured around the old Idiomatic sample’s IDMSyncManager singleton. The current Idiomatic example is a from-scratch SwiftData app, so it is not a useful migration template for those apps — map your existing sync manager’s responsibilities instead. Most of what IDMSyncManager did by hand is now built into CoreDataEnsembleContainer: IDMSyncManager responsibility Ensembles 3 equivalent +sharedSyncManager / setup Create one CoreDataEnsembleContainer at launch connectToSyncService:withCompletion: (create file system + leech) Pass the backend to the container; the first sync() attaches automatically synchronizeWithCompletion: container.sync() — and AutoSyncPolicy replaces the hand-rolled save/timer/activation triggers disconnectFromSyncServiceWithCompletion: (deleech) container.detach() persistentStoreEnsemble:didSaveMergeChangesWithNotification: (merge into main context) Handled automatically by the container’s view-context merging; use its didSaveMergeChanges callback only for extra work persistentStoreEnsemble:globalIdentifiersForManagedObjects: The container’s globalIdentifiers closure, or Syncable conformances persistentStoreEnsemble:didDeleechWithError: The container’s didForceDetach callback reset (deleech + remove local data) container.detach(); to remove the cloud data too, CoreDataEnsemble.removeEnsemble(withIdentifier:in:)  One behavioral difference to plan for: Ensembles 3 requires a source of global identifiers — the container’s globalIdentifiers closure or Syncable conformances — and refuses to attach without one (EnsembleError.missingGlobalIdentifierSource, code 220). Ensembles 2 allowed returning nil. If your IDMSyncManager already implements globalIdentifiersForManagedObjects:, port that logic; the identifiers must be stable and match what your E2 build supplied, or objects will duplicate. These steps apply equally if you are still on the open-source Ensembles 1.x: Ensembles 2 retained Ensembles 1’s cloud formats, and Ensembles 3 reads both the same way. Using Ensembles 3 from Objective-C Ensembles 3 is a Swift framework with async/await APIs and is not callable from Objective-C directly. That does not mean rewriting your app: keep the app in Objective-C, and replace the internals of your sync manager with a small Swift file that exposes an @objc interface. Your existing call sites stay untouched:  With all (the default), the explicit synchronize call is only needed where your UI wants a completion — the container already syncs on save, on a timer, and on app activation. summary: Understand how Ensembles resolves conflicts and how to customize the process.
title: Conflict Resolution
rawIndexableTextContent: Understand how Ensembles resolves conflicts and how to customize the process. Overview When multiple devices change the same data concurrently, conflicts arise. Ensembles resolves these automatically using causal revision tracking, and provides delegate hooks for cases that need custom logic. Automatic Resolution Every event carries a revision set that records which events from other peers have been seen. When events are replayed during a merge, the integrator determines the causal ordering: if one change “happened after” another (it had seen the other’s revision), that change wins. For truly concurrent changes to the same attribute, the event with the highest globalCount (a monotonically increasing counter across the device’s event history) is used as a tiebreaker. Conflict resolution operates at the attribute level: each attribute is resolved independently using last-writer-wins (LWW). For to-many relationships, Ensembles uses an add-wins set strategy — additions from both sides are preserved, and only explicit deletions are removed. Ensembles provides eventual consistency: all devices that have seen the same set of events will converge to the same state, regardless of the order in which events were received. This means that for most apps, conflicts are resolved transparently without any code on your part. The Reparation Context For cases where automatic resolution isn’t sufficient, the delegate provides a two-context pattern for inspecting and repairing merged data before it’s committed. Inspecting Changes Before the merge save, the ensemble calls:  The savingContext contains all the merged changes about to be committed. Use it to inspect what will happen:  Making Repairs Do not modify the savingContext directly. Instead, make corrections in the reparationContext:  Changes made in the reparation context are captured as new events, so they propagate to all peers on the next merge. The saving context and reparation context have a parent-child relationship. Do not nest perform or performAndWait calls between them — this will deadlock. Handling Save Failures If the merge save fails (e.g., due to a validation error), the ensemble calls:  Inspect the error to determine which objects caused the failure, make corrections in the reparationContext, and return true to reattempt the save. Return false to abort. SwiftData The reparation context operates on NSManagedObjectContext and NSManagedObject, so it isn’t directly usable from SwiftData @Model types. The recommended approach for SwiftData is to design your model so that attribute-level merging always produces valid results. See SwiftData Integration for specific strategies. Global Identifiers and Deduplication When the same logical object is created independently on multiple devices, automatic merging produces duplicates — two objects with different identifiers but the same meaning (e.g., two “Work” tags). To handle this, implement the global identifier delegate method:  When Ensembles encounters objects with matching global identifiers from different devices, it merges them into a single object rather than creating duplicates. Global identifiers must be immutable — once assigned, an object’s identifier must never change. If you need to change an identifier, delete the object and create a new one. Identifiers must also be non-empty: empty strings are a programmer error and will trip a precondition. awakeFromInsert and the Integration Context When Ensembles integrates changes from another device, it inserts and updates objects in a context of its own, and Core Data calls awakeFromInsert() on those objects just as it does for objects your code inserts. If your awakeFromInsert() assigns default content — the current location, a timestamp, a status sourced from this device — that code runs during integration too. Ensembles applies the synced attribute values after awakeFromInsert, so a value you simply assign there is normally overwritten by the synced one. The pitfall is re-applying current-device content later in the integration cycle (for example in a merge or reparation step), which can leave this device’s value in place of the synced one. To stay safe, skip current-device assignments entirely when integrating, using isEnsemblesIntegrationContext:  Assigning a stable global identifier in awakeFromInsert is fine and need not be guarded. It’s the assignment of content attributes sourced from the current device that must be skipped during integration. Forced Detaches In exceptional circumstances, the ensemble may be forced to detach: The cloud identity changed (e.g., the user signed out of iCloud) The hardware identity changed unexpectedly Data corruption was detected (incomplete mandatory events) The device’s registration was removed from the cloud When this happens, the ensemble calls coreDataEnsemble(_:didDetachWithError:). You should update your UI to reflect the detached state and can attempt to re-attach to resume syncing.

rawIndexableTextContent: Sync SwiftData models with Ensembles using SwiftDataEnsembleContainer. Overview The EnsemblesSwiftData module provides SwiftData-native APIs for Ensembles sync. You never need to touch Core Data directly — just pass your @Model types and get a syncing ModelContainer back. Complete Example: SwiftData with CloudKit Here’s a complete, working setup for a SwiftUI app that syncs SwiftData models via CloudKit. 1. Define Your Models  2. Set Up the Container  That’s the complete setup. The container creates a ModelContainer, attaches to the cloud, and syncs automatically. Your @Query properties update automatically when remote changes arrive, thanks to persistent history tracking (enabled by default). 3. Use in Views  No extra save calls needed — SwiftData auto-saves, which triggers Ensembles to sync. Using a Custom Store Location If you need control over where the SQLite file lives:  Global Identifiers with `Syncable` When two devices independently create the “same” object (e.g., a tag with the same name), Ensembles needs a global identifier to recognize they represent the same entity and merge them instead of duplicating. SwiftData models declare a global identifier by conforming to the Syncable protocol:  The globalIdentifierKey names a property whose value uniquely identifies the object across all devices. When two objects of the same entity have the same global identifier value, Ensembles merges them into one. A global identifier must never change once it has been assigned to an object. Changing an identifier after sync has begun will cause Ensembles to treat the object as a different entity, leading to duplicates or data loss. A UUID is usually the best choice for a global identifier — assign it once at creation time and it’s guaranteed unique across all devices:  Use a fixed, meaningful value instead when two devices might independently create the same logical object — for example, singleton settings objects or tags that are identified by name:  Not all entities need global identifiers — only those where independent creation of “the same” object is likely (reference data, categories, user profiles). Entities that are always created explicitly by the user (photos, drawings) typically don’t need them. Entities that do not conform to Syncable (and have no global identifier provided via a closure) are synced normally but are not deduplicated. If the same logical object is created independently on two devices, both copies will exist after sync. Auto-Sync Configuration Control when syncing occurs:  Set autoSyncPolicy to .manual and call container.sync() yourself for full control. Responding to Events  Unlike CoreDataEnsembleContainer, the SwiftData container does not need to merge changes into a view context — persistent history tracking (enabled by default) causes @Query properties to update automatically. Use didSaveMergeChanges for additional processing such as refreshing non-SwiftData UI state. Computed Identifiers (Core Data) For compound or computed identifiers on NSManagedObject subclasses, override globalIdentifier(from:) instead of globalIdentifierKey. The parameter is typed as Self, so you get direct property access:  This method is called only when globalIdentifierKey is empty (the default when you don’t override it). globalIdentifier(from:) only works with NSManagedObject subclasses. For SwiftData @Model types, use globalIdentifierKey. Conflict Resolution Ensembles resolves concurrent changes automatically using attribute-level last-writer-wins (see Conflict Resolution). For most apps this works transparently — but because each attribute is resolved independently, a merge can combine values that are individually valid but together violate a business rule (e.g., startDate from one device and endDate from another, where start ends up after end). With Core Data, you can intercept and repair these cases using the reparation context delegate methods. SwiftData models don’t have NSManagedObject subclasses, so those delegate methods aren’t directly useful. The best approach for SwiftData is to design your model so that attribute-level merging always produces valid results: Avoid cross-attribute invariants where possible. For example, store a startDate and a duration instead of startDate and endDate — either attribute can be updated independently without breaking validity. Use computed properties for derived values instead of storing them. A stored total that must equal quantity * price will break if quantity and price are updated on different devices. Compute it instead. Validate after sync by observing didSaveMergeChanges and checking invariants in your app logic. Fix invalid combinations by saving corrected values — those corrections propagate as new events. If you need the full reparation context for complex conflict handling, access the underlying CoreDataEnsemble via .coreDataEnsemble and set its delegate directly. Note that this replaces the internal delegate bridge, so you’ll need to handle global identifiers and save notifications yourself:  Using SwiftDataEnsemble Directly If you manage your own ModelContainer or need more control, use SwiftDataEnsemble directly:  Access the underlying CoreDataEnsemble via the .coreDataEnsemble property for advanced operations:  Model Versioning with VersionedSchema When you first ship your app, pass your current @Model types to modelTypes: — this is all you need for a single model version. When your model evolves (e.g., you add a property to Note), you need to tell Ensembles about all versions so it can accept sync events recorded against any of them. Do this by switching from modelTypes: to migrationPlan:. 1. Define Versioned Schemas Move your model types into VersionedSchema enums — one per version:  2. Create a Migration Plan  3. Use `migrationPlan:` Instead of `modelTypes:`  Ensembles converts each VersionedSchema into a Core Data model and passes all of them to the underlying CoreDataEnsemble. This allows version compatibility checking during sync — events from a device still running V1 can be correctly merged on a device running V2, and vice versa. Persistent History Tracking SwiftDataEnsembleContainer and SwiftDataEnsemble enable persistent history tracking by default. This allows SwiftData to detect changes that Ensembles merges into the store, so your @Query properties stay up to date automatically. Know when the app may save, how to detect sync success and failure, and how to recover a device that has fallen behind. Overview Ensembles runs alongside your app’s normal Core Data or SwiftData usage, and almost everything can happen at any time. This article covers the small set of rules that do matter: the one window in which saving causes problems, the signals that actually indicate sync success, and the recovery path for a device whose syncs keep failing. When the App May Save Saving is safe at almost any time. There is one window where a save causes real trouble, and one where it causes minor churn: During attach, a save aborts the attach with EnsembleError.saveOccurredDuringAttaching (code 206). The partial state is discarded, so nothing is corrupted, but every retry re-imports the entire store. An app that saves constantly can keep aborting its own attach indefinitely. During a merge, a save aborts that merge with EnsembleError.saveOccurredDuringMerge (code 207). The sync retries the merge a couple of times internally — the retry includes the new save’s event — and if the retries are exhausted, the merge simply reruns on the next sync trigger. This is routine in moderation; it only matters if the app saves so often that every merge window contains a save, in which case the device never completes a merge and quietly falls behind. This reduces to one practical rule: Hold writes until the first successful sync() after launch. After that, save freely. One pattern deserves a specific warning: saving in response to merged changes. If a merge-notification handler (the containers’ didSaveMergeChanges, the delegate’s equivalent, or an observer that rebuilds derived state when imported objects appear) performs a save, every merge that delivers data provokes a save, and that save aborts the next batch of the very merge that triggered it. The internal retry absorbs the occasional reactive save — the second pass delivers nothing new, so a purely reactive app converges — but a handler that saves on every pass defeats it, and the device fails every sync while its store slowly fills from the committed batches. Prefer deferring reactive writes until the sync has completed: queue them, and flush when sync() returns or on .coreDataEnsembleWillEndActivity. The first successful sync proves attach is complete. Gating on that is more dependable than checking currentActivity before saving — a sync can begin between the check and the save, so an activity-based gate cannot be made race-free from outside the framework. Coalescing frequent writes into fewer saves remains good hygiene, because it shrinks the number of merge windows a save can land in, but it is an optimization, not a correctness requirement. Detecting Success and Staleness currentActivity reports only what the ensemble is doing right now. .none means idle — it does not mean the last sync succeeded or that the device is up to date. The reliable signals are tied to a specific sync: The containers’ sync() returns true when that sync completed, false when it failed (the error goes to the container’s didEncounterError callback). sync(options:) throws on failure; returning normally means that sync succeeded. The .coreDataEnsembleWillEndActivity notification carries any error under activityError. To detect a stale device, record the time of each success and compare it against your auto-sync cadence:  Most sync errors are transient and clear on the next trigger. A device is in trouble only when the same error repeats across many attempts. Errors bridge to NSError with the domain CDEErrorDomain and the case’s raw value as the code, and their descriptions name the case, so logs are self-diagnosing. Recovering a Stale Device When one device fails every sync while the rest of the fleet is healthy: Diagnose first. Quiesce all writes, enable verbose logging with setLoggingLevel(.verbose), and run one manual sync. If it succeeds, the app was saving into every merge window — revisit the rule above. If it fails, the log names the real error. Detach and re-attach. Call the container’s detach(), then sync(). Local data is preserved and re-imported; the sync metadata is rebuilt from the cloud. This is the standard remedy. Rebuild from the cloud. If the device’s data is only a stale copy of what the cloud already holds, detach, delete the local store and local event data directory, recreate the stack, and sync. Unsynced local changes are lost, so reserve this for devices with nothing unique to keep. Forcing a rebase (forceRebase) is not a recovery tool: it compacts event history, it does not repair a failing device. For a coordinated fresh start — for example, after duplicate identities accumulated because devices attached before global identifiers were configured — de-duplicate app-side on every device, detach all devices, remove the cloud data with removeEnsemble(withIdentifier:in:), wait for the deletion to propagate, then seed the cloud from your best device before bringing in the others.

title: Architecture
rawIndexableTextContent: Understand how Ensembles synchronizes Core Data stores using event sourcing. Overview Ensembles uses an event-sourcing architecture. Every change to a Core Data persistent store is recorded as an event. Events are exchanged between devices through a pluggable cloud backend and replayed to bring each device’s store into a consistent state. Event Sourcing Model When the app saves to the monitored persistent store, a SaveMonitor captures the inserted, updated, and deleted objects and records them as a modification event in a separate event store database. Each event records the full set of property changes and is tagged with a revision that tracks causal ordering across peers. The event store is a separate SQLite database from your app’s store — Ensembles never modifies your model or schema. Events are stored locally until they are exported to the cloud, and remote events are imported and kept locally until they are integrated. The Sync Flow A call to sync(options:) proceeds through several phases: 1. Preparation The ensemble connects to the cloud backend, verifies the device’s identity (cloud account and hardware), and checks that the device is still registered. If identity has changed (e.g., the user signed out of iCloud), the ensemble forces a detach. 2. Import New data files, baselines, and events are downloaded from the cloud and stored locally. File downloads can be batched for backends that support CloudFileSystemBatchOperations. 3. Baseline Consolidation Old events are compacted into a baseline snapshot. A baseline captures the full state of the store at a point in time, allowing events before that point to be discarded. This keeps the sync data from growing without bound. 4. Rebasing When the event history grows large, the ensemble can rebase — compressing the history relative to the latest baseline. Rebasing runs automatically when Ensembles estimates a significant space saving, or can be triggered with forceRebase. 5. Integration Remote events are replayed into the persistent store in three stages: Insert — New objects are created in the store. Update — Attributes and relationships are updated. When multiple peers have changed the same attribute, the value from the most recent event (by causal ordering) wins. Delete — Objects marked as deleted are removed. Before the integrated changes are saved, the delegate can inspect and repair them via coreDataEnsemble(_:shouldSaveMergedChangesIn:reparationContext:). 6. Export New local events, baselines, and data files are uploaded to the cloud. This phase can be suppressed with suppressCloudFileDeposition. 7. Cleanup Outdated remote files (events that have been superseded by baselines) are removed from the cloud. Key Components Component Role CoreDataEnsemble Main coordinator. Serializes all operations via an internal AsyncStream. EventStore Manages the local event database (a separate SQLite database). CloudManager Orchestrates cloud file operations: snapshot, import, export, cleanup. EventIntegrator Replays remote events into the app’s persistent store. SaveMonitor Observes NSManagedObjectContextDidSave to capture local changes. RevisionManager Tracks causal ordering of events across distributed peers. BaselineConsolidator / Rebaser Consolidates event history into compact snapshots.  Cloud Backends All cloud backends implement the CloudFileSystem protocol. This is the primary extension point. See Custom Cloud Backends for a guide to adding your own. Two optional protocols extend the base: CloudFileSystemBatchOperations — Adds batch upload, download, and delete for backends that support them (reduces round trips). CloudFileSystemSetup — Adds one-time preparation, priming, and directory repair hooks. Model Versioning Each event is stamped with a model version hash (either a full entity-hash dictionary or a compressed MD5). During integration, RevisionManager checks every incoming event’s model version against the local managedObjectModels array — a list of all NSManagedObjectModel instances the app supports. When hashes match, the event is integrable and proceeds through the sync flow. When hashes don’t match, the event is flagged with EnsembleError.unknownModelVersion and excluded from integration. This prevents applying changes that reference entities or attributes the current app version doesn’t understand. Providing Model Versions For Core Data projects using .xcdatamodeld bundles, the URL-based convenience initializers on CoreDataEnsemble automatically load all model versions from the bundle via loadAllModelVersions(from:). For SwiftData projects, SwiftDataEnsemble builds in-memory models from @Model types or VersionedSchema entries. You can also pass managedObjectModels directly to the designated initializer when you have in-memory models from other sources. The `managedObjectModels` Array If managedObjectModels is nil, model version checking is disabled and all events are treated as integrable. This is appropriate for testing but not recommended in production. If the array is non-nil, it must contain all model versions that any peer in the sync group might produce. When a peer upgrades its schema and starts emitting events with a new model hash, other peers must also be updated to include that model version or they will reject those events. Handling Breaking Migrations Ensembles does not perform Core Data model migration itself — it only checks compatibility. If you add or rename entities or attributes, you must: Include both the old and new NSManagedObjectModel in the managedObjectModels array. Perform any necessary lightweight or custom migration on the app’s persistent store before attaching the ensemble. Ensure all peers in the sync group are updated to understand the new schema before they sync events from upgraded peers. Data Flow Diagram  Local saves flow right: captured by the event store, then exported to the cloud. Remote changes flow left: imported from the cloud into the event store, then integrated into the app’s store.
